draftNotes:
Introduction

The Constitution lets the President turn the armed forces outward against an enemy. It does not let him reach into a working federal prosecution, take a lawfully present resident out of it, and hold him offshore on evidence no judge has seen. Congress wrote detention rules, left Bronner’s category out, and has twice refused to fill it in. We ask this court to reverse for 3 reasons.

The ladder (say this in the roadmap)

  1. Lowest ebb. He acted against what Congress decided. Youngstown Category 3.
  2. Even in Category 2 (if the court finds Congress silent), Article II alone does not reach a man arrested at his own house. Jackson: force "turned inward" gets no indulgence.
  3. Even with authority, the process fails. Hamdi = notice + chance to rebut before a neutral decisionmaker. 12 months, no charge, sealed evidence (R. 7–8).

Lose 1, still win on 2. Lose 2, still win on 3. Hamdi itself split this way (authority for the government, process for the detainee), so 3 is the most winnable rung.

Shorthand key

  • R. = PDF page of record. App. = appendix (R. 20–25). FN = footnote.
  • AUMF = 2001 force authorization. NDAA = 2012 defense act §§ 1021–1022. ATA = 2025 Anti-Terrorist Act § 4. EO = Executive Order 15,000, signed 14 Feb 2025. LPR = lawful permanent resident = Bronner.
  • "Nothing affects existing law" clause: cite App. III. Body misattributes it at R. 3.

c3-s0.title: Opening theme
c3-s0.notes:
Courtroom, not battlefield

  1. Arrested at his house by civilian agents. Arraigned in an Article III court 30 May 2025, pled not guilty, released on bond (R. 8)
    • Handed to the military 7 July, flown to Guantanamo (R. 8)
    • => civilian process was not unavailable. It had already started and it was working
  2. Posture decides the burden
    • Judge Fair granted the writ, then stayed it. Fourteenth Circuit reversed. Review de novo, jurisdiction stipulated (R. 2, R. 9)
    • Jackson: Category 1 action carries "the strongest of presumptions" and the burden rests heavily on the challenger
    • The majority put him in Category 1 and then asked Bronner to beat a presumption Congress never created
  3. The two three-day gaps (framing, not bad faith)
    • EO signed 14 Feb 2025. USCIS approved naturalization 17 Feb on an express good moral character finding (R. 4)
    • Oath set for 4 July. Flown to Guantanamo 7 July (R. 8)
    • Do not argue a setup. The warehouse evidence surfaced in late May. Argue: the government’s own file called him good moral character months into the period it now calls him a belligerent
  4. One theory for both questions
    • Keith (United States v. U.S. District Court, 1972, warrantless domestic security wiretaps): the Fourth Amendment does not treat "the executive officers of government as neutral and disinterested magistrates"
    • Q1: nobody outside the executive approved the surveillance. Q2: nobody outside the executive has tested the belligerency label

c3-s1.title: 1) Lowest ebb: The president acted against Congress
c3-s1.notes:
Framework

Youngstown Sheet & Tube v. Sawyer, 343 U.S. 579 (1952) = the steel seizure case. Truman seized the mills during a wartime strike, told Congress twice, Congress did nothing, seizure held unconstitutional. Jackson’s concurrence is the test everyone uses.

  1. Category 1 = Congress authorized it. Power at maximum.
  2. Category 2 = "zone of twilight". Congress neither granted nor denied. Depends on circumstances.
  3. Category 3 = Congress said no, expressly or by implication. Power at its "lowest ebb" (= weakest). Survives only if the subject is beyond Congress’s reach entirely.

=> Detention is plainly not beyond Congress’s reach. It legislated on it in 2011 (NDAA) and again in 2025 (ATA).

c3-s1-a.title: a. Jackson’s method, not just his labels
c3-s1-a.notes:
Walk the three steps he walked

  1. Category 1 out: the government conceded Congress never authorized the seizure
  2. Category 2 out: Congress had not "left seizure of private property an open field". It had enacted three labour-emergency mechanisms and Truman used none
    • The quote to use: in "choosing a different and inconsistent way of his own", the President "cannot claim that it is necessitated or invited by failure of Congress to legislate"
  3. => Category 3, and the seizure failed

Do the same three steps with our statutes. Then the category is a conclusion we earned, not a label we asserted.

Three Jackson passages that do work here

  • Force turned inward. "Widest latitude" for command of national force "turned against the outside world", no such indulgence when turned inward. Arrested at home, arraigned in federal court => inward
  • Only delegated powers. The executive "possesses only delegated powers"; the Vesting Clause is not "a grant in bulk of all conceivable executive power". This answers the half of their case that cites no statute at all (R. 12)
  • Commander in Chief = "cryptic words"; nothing "more sinister and alarming" than a President who could "vastly enlarge his mastery over the internal affairs of the country". No "monopoly of war powers"

Best quote in the record

At the EO signing: inherent foreign affairs and war powers allow him to act "beyond any specific law or statutory framework" (R. 3–4).

=> That is Category 3 described by the man claiming the power. He is not saying Congress authorized this.

Kill "sole organ" before they say it

  • Majority relies on Curtiss-Wright, 299 U.S. 304 (1936): "sole organ", "plenary and exclusive" (R. 12)
  • Answer = Youngstown FN2 (Jackson), which addressed that case directly: it involved "not the question of the President’s power to act without congressional authority, but the right to act under and in accord with an Act of Congress", and much of it was dictum
  • => the answer comes from inside the case they picked

What they say back

The neutrality clauses (NDAA §§ 1021(d), 1021(e); ATA § 4(c)) say nothing limits or expands existing presidential authority => Category 2 at worst. That is a real argument. It is why prong b exists.

c3-s1-b.title: b. Even if in 2nd ebb - Silence is not permission
c3-s1-b.notes:
b. Even if in Category 2, silence is not permission

They cannot point to a grant, so they point to 4 substitutes: a disclaimer, an affirmation, silence, and his own say-so. None is a grant. Keith says we cannot use Congress’ inaction as authority.

  1. a. The framework we must use: Keith, a disclaimer is not a grant
    1. Government relied on Title III § 2511(3): "nothing in this Act limits the President’s power" to protect against overthrow of the government
    2. Held: "merely a disclaimer of congressional intent", not a grant of authority
    3. Identical sentence structure in all three clauses they cite: NDAA § 1021(d), § 1021(e), ATA § 4(c)
      1. Not a grant there => not a grant here
    4. Dissent used Keith only on the warrant question (R. 17). Extending it to Article II is the biggest upgrade available to us
  2. b. Their affirmative text only describes a power, it does not create one
    1. § 1021(a): Congress "affirms" that existing authority includes detaining covered persons. It does not "grant" (App. III, R. 21)
    2. A provision describing a power the drafters assumed already existed cannot be its source
  3. c. Acquiescence does not apply (3 reasons)
    1. Costanzo v. Tillinghast, 287 U.S. 341 (1932) = a deportation case about punctuation in an immigration statute (R. 13)
    2. Costanzo’s own requirements are absent here
      1. consistent agency reading
      2. published in successive rulebooks over ~15 years
      3. Congress declining to amend
      4. => nothing in this record looks like that
    3. Majority concedes it was immigration administration, then asserts the principle "applies equally" = assertion, not argument
  4. d. Their legislative history proves the opposite
    1. Senate bills barring indefinite detention failed (R. 2–3); AUMF repeal votes in 2023 and 2025 never taken up in the House (R. 3)
      1. => all it proves is that nothing passed
      2. A failed bill does not enact its opposite
    2. The fact that wins this prong: in 2026 the House passed a bill authorizing offshore detention of lawfully present non-citizens with no criminal record. Still pending in the Senate (R. 3)
      1. => Congress is deciding right now whether to grant the power he says he already has
      2. => no acquiescence from a legislature still debating
  5. e. His own say-so is not law
    1. Black’s majority: power must come from an Act of Congress or from the Constitution, and lawmaking belongs to Congress
    2. A presidential statement about the scope of his own power is evidence of the claim, not of the authority
    3. Pairs with R. 3–4: acts "beyond any specific law or statutory framework"

Bench note, not an argument

Non-Detention Act, 18 U.S.C. § 4001(a) is not in our appendices (R. 20–25 = AUMF, § 948(a)(7), NDAA §§ 1021–1022, ATA, EO 15,000). Check the outside-authority rule before relying on it.

c3-s1-c.title: c. Where the line actually falls
c3-s1-c.notes:
The line is not citizenship and not place of arrest

It is: were the civilian courts open, and has anyone neutral tested the label.

Milligan is the structural case

  • Ex parte Milligan, 71 U.S. 2 (1866) = Indiana civilian and Confederate sympathiser, tried by military commission. Indiana was never a theatre of war, courts open. Commission had no jurisdiction
  • Bronner is stronger than Milligan: his court was not just open in the abstract, it had arraigned him and bonded him out before the military took him (R. 8)

Quirin is their best case. Narrow it, do not fight it

  • Ex parte Quirin, 317 U.S. 1 (1942) = eight German-trained saboteurs off submarines, buried their uniforms, one a U.S. citizen. Commission upheld. Majority uses it at R. 12
  • Concede citizenship and domestic arrest are not disqualifying. We lose both
  • Narrow the way the dissent did (R. 18): sent by a foreign nation in a declared war, status rested on proven conduct not accusation, and Quirin distinguished Milligan rather than overruling it

A definition is not a grant

  • "Unprivileged enemy belligerent" comes from 10 U.S.C. § 948(a)(7) = a definition inside a military commissions chapter (App. II, R. 20)
  • It says who may be tried by commission. It authorizes nobody to detain anybody
  • Of four subparts only (B), purposeful and material support of hostilities, is arguably in reach on these facts
  • => the majority’s whole Article II chain starts by applying that label (R. 12), so it rests on a definitional provision doing work it was never written for

Use the Prize Cases for their limits

  • 67 U.S. 635 (1863): Lincoln’s blockade upheld, no need to "wait for Congress to baptize it with a name". Majority quotes this at R. 12
  • But: armed attack in progress, organised forces, and a blockade that necessarily ended when the war ended
  • => that conflict had an endpoint. This one has none, which is exactly why open-ended detention under it is different

Who applies the label

The AG applied it on sealed evidence Bronner has never seen (R. 7–8). Keith = why that is a problem. Ties back to force turned inward.

c3-s2.title: 2) The statutes exclude him
c3-s2.notes:
Strategy

Concede Hamdi on its own facts immediately. It costs nothing and buys credibility. Then show each statute either leaves his category out or authorizes something other than what happened.

The four sources they stack

  • AUMF (Sept 2001): force against those responsible for 9/11
  • NDAA FY2012 §§ 1021–1022: detention of "covered persons"
  • ATA (early 2025) § 4: detention rules by category of person
  • EO 15,000 (14 Feb 2025): directs the AG to detain certain non-citizens outside the continental U.S.

c3-s2-a.title: a. AUMF + NDAA §§ 1021–1022
c3-s2-a.notes:
Hamdi: concede, then confine

  • Hamdi v. Rumsfeld, 542 U.S. 507 (2004) = U.S. citizen seized in Afghanistan, alleged Taliban fighter, held with no charge, no counsel, no hearing, government’s whole case was one short DoD declaration
  • Authority: AUMF permitted it. Detention for the duration is "a fundamental incident of waging war"
  • Process: still inadequate. "A state of war is not a blank check for the President" (542 U.S. at 535; dissent extends to LPRs at R. 17)
  • Their two distinctions: citizen, and captured in a combat zone. The first cuts against us. The second cuts for us, harder: the further from a battlefield, the weaker the case for battlefield rules

AUMF § 2(a) is narrow on its own text

  • Force against nations, organizations, or persons the President determines planned, authorized, committed, or aided 9/11, or harboured them, to prevent future terrorism "by such nations, organizations, or persons" (App. I, R. 20)
  • That closing phrase loops prevention back to the same actors => not a general counterterrorism authority
  • Nothing in the record ties Bronner to the 9/11 perpetrators

§ 1021(b)(2) is the tightest constraint in the scheme

  • Covered person = was "part of" or "substantially supported" al-Qaeda, the Taliban, or associated forces engaged in hostilities against the U.S.
  • Record gives us: Roper and Langbourne questioned about suspected ties to organizations involved in drug smuggling (R. 7)
  • => several inferential steps short of the element, and it describes the sellers, not Bronner

§ 1021(c)(1) is a clock, not just a power

Detention under the law of war "until the end of hostilities" authorized by the AUMF. Both repeal attempts failed and the AUMF is still law (R. 3) => on their reading the clock never runs out. An authority that cannot expire is a reason to read it narrowly.

§ 1022 carve-outs, stated fairly

  • (a) requires military custody for certain captured people. (b)(1) excludes U.S. citizens. (b)(2) excludes "lawful resident aliens" for conduct inside the U.S., "except to the extent permitted by the Constitution" (App. IV, R. 22)
  • With § 1021(e) preserving existing law for citizens and LPRs captured in the U.S. => Congress singled out exactly his group for protection
  • Their answer is fair: the carve-outs lift an obligation, not a power. The military need not take these people, not may not. That reading is textually available, so do not stake the prong on ours being the only one. Win it through Keith and through ATA structure in prong b

The point most people miss: § 1022(a)(4)

  • The President may waive military custody by certifying to Congress in writing that the waiver is in the national security interest
  • => Congress built a mechanism and a reporting duty into this exact subject, and the record contains no such certification
  • This is Jackson’s step two almost word for word: Congress supplied a route, he took "a different and inconsistent way of his own"
  • Say "the record contains no certification", not "none exists"

c3-s2-b.title: b. ATA § 4 shows what Congress chose
c3-s2-b.notes:
Claim

Congress wrote express offshore rules for the category above him and the category below him, left his category blank, then twice refused to fill it in.

What § 4 says

  • 4(a) AG may direct the DOJ to detain any person present in the U.S. suspected of terrorism. No location specified
  • 4(b)(1) unlawfully present + suspected: detained inside the U.S., or outside if the President expressly orders it after finding the detainee would be at risk or a risk to others if held inside
  • 4(b)(2) citizens may be detained but must be held inside the territorial jurisdiction. No offshore authority for citizens at all
  • Lawfully present non-citizens (= him): nothing (App. V, R. 23–24; R. 3)

Strongest textual point available, and it is easy to miss

  • § 4(a) authorizes the AG to direct the DOJ to detain. The ATA is a Justice Department custody statute. Nothing in § 4 authorizes handing anyone to the armed forces
  • Military custody comes only from NDAA § 1022, and § 1022 is the one provision that carves out LPRs
  • => the two statutes they stack point opposite ways. The one covering the custody he is actually in excludes him; the one that might cover him names a different custodian

Jackson’s step two, applied

  • Detailed rules for two groups + rejected offshore-detention provisions for citizens in 2025 and 2026 + the 2026 LPR bill still in the Senate (R. 3)
  • => offshore detention is not "an open field"

What § 4 leaves out (R. 3)

  • No time limit. No required dangerousness finding. No guaranteed counsel. No judicial review provision
  • Counts twice: on category, Congress was not authorizing an open-ended regime. On process, there is no statutory substitute for the Hamdi hearing

c3-s2-c.title: c. EO 15,000 concedes its own limits
c3-s2-c.notes:
The order undercuts their Category 1 claim

  • § 3: to be implemented "consistent with applicable law" (App. VI, R. 25)
  • => an order conceding it operates within the statutes cannot be the source of a power that exceeds them
  • Direct answer to the majority at R. 14 ("the ATA further illuminates the grant of authority"), especially paired with the DOJ / military custody mismatch above

How it was applied to him

  • AG classified him as a removable non-citizen "with a criminal record" because he had been accused of a federal crime. He has no convictions (R. 8)
  • => misuse of the term, and it shows how little testing the label gets
  • Be honest: the order separately covers non-citizens with pending charges, and he had pending charges. Its terms are arguably satisfied even though the stated reason is wrong. Attack the reasoning and the error risk. Do not claim it could never reach him

c3-s3.title: 3) Even with authority, the process fails
c3-s3.notes:
Why this rung matters most

Hamdi split exactly here: government won authority, detainee won process. This is the rung most likely to produce an actual win even if the court rejects 1 and 2.

The rule

Hamdi, applying Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319 (1976) (a Social Security disability case, relevant only because Hamdi borrowed its three-factor balancing): a detainee held on an enemy-combatant classification must get notice of the factual basis and a meaningful opportunity to rebut it before a neutral decisionmaker.

c3-s3-a.title: a. The three Mathews factors
c3-s3-a.notes:
1. Private interest

  • Hamdi: freedom from physical restraint = "the most elemental of liberty interests"
  • 12 months in military custody at Guantanamo, no charge (R. 7–8)

2. Risk of error = our strongest ground

  • Magistrate found probable cause, federal court arraigned him, federal judge released him on bond, all before the military took him (R. 8; dissent R. 19)
  • USCIS approved naturalization on an express good moral character finding 3 days after the EO (R. 4)
  • No convictions, and the stated basis for the belligerent label was that he had been accused (R. 8)
  • => the risk is not hypothetical. Two neutral decisionmakers already looked at this man and neither reached their conclusion

3. Government interest

  • They say the evidence is too sensitive and they intend to prosecute "as soon as practicable" (R. 8, R. 14)
  • Answer with the dissent (R. 18): they have not shown why sensitivity prevents a neutral tribunal from testing the classification, as opposed to preventing full public disclosure. Only the second is at stake

c3-s3-b.title: b. Answer their habeas / Banyee close
c3-s3-b.notes:
What the majority says (R. 14)

Due process is satisfied because habeas is available and working, there is no six-month ceiling, and no individualised determination is required absent evidence of a ruse, citing Banyee v. Garland, 115 F.4th 928, 934 (8th Cir. 2024).

Three-track reply

  1. Habeas tests whether the detention is lawful, not whether the factual classification behind it is accurate
  2. A habeas court cannot meaningfully test facts the detainee has never been allowed to see (R. 7–8)
  3. Banyee = prolonged immigration detention under established removal procedures. Different liberty interest, different error risk from offshore military custody on an untested belligerency label

The citizenship answer

Hamdi frames its process holding for a citizen and they will lean on that. The Fifth Amendment says person, not citizen, and LPRs inside the U.S. have long been held to have due process rights.

c3-s3-c.title: c. Remedy
c3-s3-c.notes:
Primary

  • Affirm the grant of the writ and order him released from military custody back into the pending criminal case
  • He was arraigned and pled not guilty, so there is a live prosecution to return to
  • Say this out loud. The bench’s unspoken worry is that ruling for us frees a man who tried to buy a radiological weapon. Answer: the criminal process still exists and still works

Fallback

  • If the court finds authority, take the dissent’s remedy (R. 18): remand for a hearing with notice of the factual basis and a chance to rebut before a neutral decisionmaker, plus periodic review so "duration of hostilities" does not become permanent

=> a narrow second ask makes the broad first ask easier to grant.

c3-s4.title: Concessions + preservation
c3-s4.notes:
Not preserved, stay away

  • No treaty or protocol claims. No speedy trial, bail, or innocence-of-the-evidence claims (R. 9 n.9). Record states the rule that issues not raised below are not preserved (R. 2)
  • Government never asserted independent probable cause; Bronner never challenged the warrant itself. Neither preserved (R. 9 n.8)
  • => that is why the stipulation that they relied "primarily" on the pole-camera footage carries so much weight on Q1 (R. 7)

Concede early

  • Quirin: citizenship and domestic arrest are not disqualifying. Move the fight to the untested label and the open courtroom
  • Hamdi authorizes detention on its own facts
  • NDAA §§ 1021(a) and 1021(c)(1) are affirmative text and their best card. Say so

Treat as settled even where the maths is odd

93 days of surveillance is stipulated. Install 18 March to warrant 27 May is 70 days (R. 5, R. 7), but the record says 93 three times and both opinions accept it. Opening that door gains nothing.

Record inconsistencies to know first

  • Dissenting judge: "Cassady" in the panel line (R. 2), "Cassidy" in the dissent heading (R. 16). Pick one, say the record spells it both ways if asked
  • District of Olympus (R. 2, R. 8) vs Central District of Olympus (R. 9)
  • "Nothing affects existing law" clause: § 1022(e) at R. 3, § 1021(e) per the dissent at R. 18. App. III puts it at 1021(e); App. IV has no (e) at all. Cite App. III

One framing discipline

The dissent agrees with us, which makes it tempting to lean on. But cert was granted with no circuit split on Q1. Argue the reasoning on its own terms, not that the dissent was right.
